summary: Gives an overview of security considerations when moving from IPv4 to coexisting IPv4 and IPv6 networks, grouped into issues from the IPv6 protocol, from transition mechanisms, and from deployment. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4942 surveys security issues that arise when IPv4 and IPv6 run at the same time. It covers IPv6 features, tunnels and other transition tools, and practical deployment choices that network operators need to account for.

questions: what are ipv6 transition security issues
why are ipv6 routing headers dangerous
what security issues arise during ipv6 transition
subtitle: A survey of security issues when IPv6 operates alongside IPv4 and transition mechanisms.

tldr.problem: Networks that add IPv6 while retaining IPv4 must manage security risks from both protocols, transition mechanisms, and deployment choices.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC groups concerns into protocol features, transition mechanisms, and operational deployment. It discusses risks and possible filtering or configuration responses.
tldr.outcome: The document is an overview, not a standard. It advises careful IPv6 security design and notes that some filtering choices can also block unusual legitimate traffic.

today: RFC 4942 is Informational and was published in September 2007. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Coexistence Needs Security Planning
sections.content:
The RFC expects IPv6 to be added alongside IPv4 rather than replace it immediately. It estimates that IPv6 capabilities could take two or three equipment replacement cycles, or nine to 15 years, to spread through the network. Dual-protocol operation and transition security therefore remain relevant during that period.

The memo groups its overview into issues caused by IPv6 itself, by transition mechanisms, and by IPv6 deployment. It also discusses IPv6 address probing and privacy concerns that it considers wrongly identified as security problems.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 and IPv6 may operate together for an extended transition. Operators need to protect both protocols and any mechanisms that connect them.

sections.title: Risks in IPv6 Headers and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
Routing headers can let a packet's later destination differ from the address checked by an access-control device. The RFC says devices enforcing destination rules need to examine both the base-header destination and any remaining routing-header destinations. It also discusses ICMPv6 responses to multicast packets, bogus ICMPv6 errors, and site-scope multicast addresses.

Extension headers complicate inspection because a middlebox may need to parse a chain that includes headers it does not recognize. Fragmentation creates further risks: the RFC says firewalls should drop overlapping fragments and suggests considering dropping non-final fragments smaller than 640 octets. Neighbor Discovery and Router Advertisements also need protection against unauthenticated local senders.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 routing and extension headers can make packet filtering more difficult. Operators need policies for unknown headers, fragments, Neighbor Discovery, and Router Advertisements.

sections.title: Addressability, Tunnels, and Transition Tools
sections.content:
IPv6 provides end-to-end addressability, but it does not require unrestricted end-to-end connectivity. Firewalls can still control traffic. The RFC recommends that organizations avoid treating NAT as their only security boundary and warns against using NAT-PT as a general transition mechanism.

Tunnels can bypass ingress filtering and expose tunnel endpoints to packets from sources that were not previously configured. Automatic tunnels and relays raise additional trust and denial-of-service concerns. The RFC recommends filtering tunneled traffic at the IPv4 firewall before decapsulation and again at the IPv6 firewall.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 addresses do not prevent an organization from controlling connections with firewalls. Tunnel traffic needs security checks both before and after decapsulation.

sections.title: Operational Deployment Issues
sections.content:
An IPv6 pilot can appear less secure than an existing IPv4 service if hosts and routers lack IPv6 firewall rules. The RFC warns that IPv6 may be enabled by default in equipment, and that administrators should check whether access controls cover both protocols.

Other deployment concerns include easy-to-guess interface identifiers, multiple addresses per host, reduced-function devices, IPsec traffic that perimeter devices cannot inspect, and insecure defaults. ICMPv6 cannot simply be blocked wholesale because IPv6 functions depend on it. The RFC advises logging dropped traffic and reviewing the results.
sections.plainLanguage: Apply security policy to IPv6 when enabling it, including on devices with default settings. Keep the ICMPv6 messages that IPv6 needs and review traffic that filtering blocks.

sections.title: The Memo's Scope and Advice
sections.content:
RFC 4942 brings together security considerations from IPv6 specifications, transition mechanisms, and operational experience. It does not define a new protocol. Its filtering recommendations aim to reduce malicious traffic while recognizing that unusual but valid packets may also be dropped.

The memo recommends configurable filtering and review of dropped-packet logs. It also explains that privacy addresses and the size of IPv6 address space do not automatically create the probing risks sometimes attributed to them; predictable tunnel addressing can change that assessment.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a security overview rather than a protocol specification. Its advice is to configure IPv6 controls carefully and check whether those controls block legitimate traffic.
